links.reason: 349 has Vijayai remove garland and necklace while her hair laments (புலம்ப); only the removing of ornaments, not the hair, is stated and no cutting. 2637 is the matrons plucking their hair (பறித்தனர்), other women; 'the same hair' is false and the pair is only a shared motif of hair and renunciation.

3105 pictures desire as grass (புற்கற்றை) luring into the four-state pen and says reaching the pure one's feet (நிருமலன் பாதஞ் சேரின்) lets one go to release; Kural 10 has the feet and the sea of births. The verse has no sea, so the 'swim' gain is not in it, and the Kural does not gain a reason for being in the sea from a pen image.

The note says the onlookers name leprosy and that the doer is shown eating then rotting; 217 has neither, only உம்மை வல்வினை, இம்மைச் செய்த வினைப்பயன், and karma that does not die (பொன்றினும் பொன்றல). The gain 'without needing a past birth' contradicts line 1's உம்மை, a former birth.

The verses make no incompatible claim: 34 says the konrai flute is sweet enough that the asunam sleeps, 1228 says the woman finds the herdsman's flute (குழல்) a weapon. The shared flute and the listener's state is a fair contrast, but 'limit on the land's contentment' is not in 34, so the gains are overdrawn.

Both are Kayamanar's foster-mother poems of the elopement, but they are separate poems; 17 does not place her at home (she imagines the feet on the waste, 'வல்லகொல் செல்ல'), so 'two stages' is imposed. 'The poet built the mother as a figure moving through a story' is not shown by two independent poems.

2748 only lists topics of the sermon (அருமையின் எய்தும் யாக்கை, யாக்கைய தழிவு) and states no view, while 307 calls life and body a support (உறுதுணை). Two verses sharing the word body do not make the Jain sage hold that the body 'must end' against a Saiva support; no claim is set against a claim.

The patikam's closing renunciation of the wives, brother and friends and the verse of Civakan's end by refusing food (கையினை மறித்துக் கொள்ளான்) are related as summary and scene. But 3073 is flagged uncertain, does not say the wives still wait, and 'the cost' is the reader's gloss; a generous reading.

347 names an ஊழ்வினை of a former birth (உம்மை) as the cause of Vijayai's distress and 2763 has ஊழ்வினை துரப்ப; rule and case do pair. But 2763 does not say 'all who do evil'; the palm-fruit simile is hard, and the pair mostly shares the word ஊழ்வினை.

1040 has the maiden pray that the disease of birth (பிறவிநோய்) leave her; 1049 has a friend urge her to take even the state without birth and death (சாதலும் பிறத்தலுமிலாத தானம்) as husk (கோது). They do set opposite values on release, but the friend's line is lover's hyperbole, not a claim the work holds, so the conflict is thin.

866 has learned men fix the hour for the bride to board; 958 has two kings meet at the hour the astrologers set (கணிவரை பொழுதினால்). The shared reliance on the astrologers' hour is only a theme, and neither answers or fulfils the other; they are two points in the wedding sequence.

134 has delicate feet shivering on flowering cotton, 1120 has anicham and swan's down like nerunji fruit to her feet: both use the tenderness-of-feet conceit. 'Turned into description' asserts a history of borrowing the Tamil does not show, and line 1 of 134 is hard, so the gains overstate.
links.text_issue: line 1 குஞ்சி மேல் அனிச்ச hard; sense flagged

links.reason: 1165 makes pride born from the fire called anger (சினமெனப் பட்ட தீ) and the sword thirsty for blood, but the warrior never says anger is good; Kural 306 has anger burn the raft of kin (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணை). The shared fire image is real, but a praise of anger that contradicts the Kural is read in.

946 promises நற்கதி to a dying dog who takes the five padas; 905 says that by chanting சிவாயநம no birth follows. Different promises to different hearers for different situations are not an incompatible claim; the five-ness is a shared number and the note itself concedes the Jain verse promises only a good birth.

195 has the king linger (வைகும்) with his wife like a monsoon cloud and 198 says he slipped from guarding the land (மண் அகம் காவலின் வழுக்கி). The note is accurate, but the two are neighbouring verses in one scene and 198 states the lapse outright, so it is sequence plus a poet's aside, not an answer to 195.

785 has the king's hunters and drummers guard the forest (கானகங் காக்கும்); 742 lists a shady forest among a fort's parts. The note says the verse 'lacks the idea that the forest is itself a defence', which 785 does not need, and the pair shares only the word forest.

126 lists what desire destroys (காம மென்றான்); 360 says pain ends when desire, anger and confusion lose their names. The note's claim that the king 'begins the cure by leaving the court' is not in the verse, and the second gain (what the removed desire costs) misdescribes 126, which lists the cost of desire kept.

2811 says all who have taken a body suffer (யாக்கைகொண் டவர்கட்கு) and even gods are subject to higher gods; Naladiyar 173 says parting, illness and ruin come to all embodied and bids the heart cling to the wise. The extension to the gods is real, but the epic verse offers no remedy and the quatrain does not 'need' the extension, so teaches and gains overreach.

1527 has a household member address the house deity (இல்லுறை தெய்வம்); 1531 has Kemasari ask the bees to be gods worthy of worship (தொழுதகு தெய்வமாவீர்). Both are deity addresses in one scene, but nothing says the household 'turned to the deity for her survival' and 1531 is flagged uncertain; this is a scene sequence, not a shared image doing work.

Naladiyar 101 already has the old deed (பழவினை) seek out the doer like a calf its mother, which implies carry-over across births; the claim that the quatrain does not reach past the doer's body is not shown. 217's வினைப்பயன் and 'does not die though she die' do add persistence, but the gains overstate the difference.

878 asks what cause joins the elements (பூதங்கள் சேர்வதற்கு ஏது), mocking the materialist; 1805 says maya that does not know and the elements it makes are grace's fivefold work. 878 does not say the cause lies in the soul and its deeds, and 1805 says nothing of unknowing matter failing to assemble into a knower, so 'both deny' is read in. No gains line was given.

1111 has her shame-cage (நாண் என்னுங் கன்னிச் சிறை) break in his embrace; 1122 has him say that even sitting on his lap she looks like a stranger (ஏதிலாள் போலும்) and he knows not how to live while his beloved is shy (மாதரா ணாணும்). The later verse limits the earlier claim that shame is gone, which is a real qualification, though 1111's figure is loose.

27 has Sathanikan give the throne to Udayanan and become an ascetic; 2883 has a king advise guarding the realm, giving it to a son and only then renouncing. The same order of duties appears, but 'follows the order the Cintamani lays down' implies a dependence the verses do not show, and the 'two named sons' are not in 27.

2929 shows beggars who never gave (கொடுத்துண் டறியாதார்) and 2624 a once-rich woman begging, her fall put to வெவ்வினை. They are parallel exempla under the sermon's refrain, not one extending the other; and 2624 blames cruel deeds, not a 'turn of fortune'.

Natrinai 8 has the neythal of Poraiyan's Thondi bloom like eyes (கண் போல் நெய்தல்) in the man's first wonder at her; Akananuru 290 has her eyes lose the beauty of the cool neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi (மணிஏர் மாண்நலம் ஒரீஇ). The flower-eye pair runs in opposite directions at found and lost beauty, and both name the Chera port Thondi, so the pairing teaches something neither poem shows alone.

986 has Prajapati say the lad who wins her will surely rule the wheel (அருமைகொ டிகிரி யாள்தற் கையமொன் றில்லை); 1127 has singers call her ஆழியாள்வான் பெருந்தேவி, the wheel-ruler's chief queen. The later song takes the earlier declaration as already true, so the verse fulfils the prediction in the singers' mouths, though 'first coronation' is figurative.

540 shows the king keeping the suitors waiting and hiding his intent (கரந்து வைத்தான்) after trusting the astrologer's word; Kural 376 says what is not one's portion stays not (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம்). That the portion lies in Rajamapuram is not in 540, and the king's management of suitors is not in the Kural's scope; the connection rests on unseen context.

2548 has women call him a lion fed by Kandukkan (கந்துகன் வளர்த்த சிங்கம்); 473 has the foster father receive him. Only the foster father's name joins them, and 'the credential of the merchant rearing in the city's praise' is the note's own reading; 473's closing formula is itself doubtful.

670 has the king stand ready to kill Civakan, burning like the god who ate poison; 455 has an unnamed one rage on hearing the herd recovered. That the raging man is the king is a reading from the story (the marker admits it), so the note's chain from fame to murder plan rests on that identification.

1735 names the boy அமித தேசன் for boundless might (அளப்பருந் திறல்); 1791 has him enter outshining the kings. The name's meaning and his brightness are matched in words, but nothing in 1735 'promises' he will outshine kings at a swayamvara; the pair is a name and a later use of it.

1 says the lord's feet are praised so that release be taught by leaving cruel deeds (வெவ்வினை); 139 has the king refuse to take a life to guard his own, on the grounds that kings are the shield of lives. The refusal is on kingly grounds, not release, and 'first such act' is unshown; the pair is a theme match, not an enacted promise.

1928 has the lion fall into the hunters' net after leaping without judgment; Kural 500 has the jackal kill the fearless elephant where the feet sink (காலாழ் களர்). The Kural's point is ground, the epic's is rash resolve, and lines 1-2 of 1928 are a hard simile; 'the net is the place chosen by weaker men' is not in the verse.

305 has the speaker say his deeds caused his parents hard pain in every birth and cast beings into hell (நரகின் வீழ்க்கும் வினை); Kural 320 says pains rest on those who caused pain. The verse confesses harm done, but the return of pain to him is only implied by 'what shall I do', and the picture is a virtue-illustration of the Kural, not a development.

1305 has Kamukan come learned in all arts (கற்றவன் கலைகளெல்லாம்) bearing bow and arrow; 1306 has the volley turned aside and the archer shot down. These are consecutive verses of one fight, and the plot already records the order; 'learning made good' is the note's gloss.

The note says 2005 shows Suramanjari's heart rising to sink into his chest; the verse names her only as the swooning beauty (சோருங் காரிகை சுரமஞ்சரி) and the mind that rises (உள்ளம் உடன்றெழுகின்றதே) longing for her breasts is the one who longs to bathe, which the marker takes as Civakan's. The condition in 908 is her vow, so 2005 does not show it met by her longing.

1861 is Civakan's self-curse if he does not bring the raiders to the king with crowns at his feet; 1864 has all the companions (தோழரெல்லாம்) fall at Civakan's feet and be honoured, ending their grief (அவலநோய்). These are his own companions, not the raiders, so the note's 'raiders ride into the city honoured' is unsupported, and no incompatible claim exists.

16 has townspeople say an angered goddess brings disease and takes lives (தேவி சிந்தை சிதைத்தனள் சீறுமேல்); Siddhar 1473 says the Pidari sacrifice of goat and cock does not cure and the family deity does not deform you. A reported folk belief against its rejection is a defensible tension, but 1473 is flagged uncertain and may be ironic, the goddess in 16 is not the family deity, and the human-sacrifice gain is not in either verse.
links.text_issue: Siddhar verse sense uncertain, possibly ironic

links.reason: 223's dream has the பிண்டி fall (தொலைந்து அற வீழ்ந்தது) and 271 names the Jina by the same tree (பிண்டி வாமன்). The marker itself says the tree is both a royal and a religious emblem; the epithet is a stock name, so the claim that one tree 'carries the loss and the remedy' is an attractive reading, not a clearly shared image.

417 has a hunter dismiss the chariot-man (ஒருவன் என்செயும்) and urge the raid; 450 has the hunters curse the omen-reader as having lied (பொய்த்தான்) once the chariots surround them. A boast and the scene that refutes it is a real within-epic link, but it is not an incompatible claim, and the 'omen' was not the dismissed warning in 417.

The note says Soolamani wins the state 'by its own meditation'; 2125 mentions no meditation or effort, only casting off the coverings (ஆவரண நீக்கி) and standing in சிவகதி. With no claim about means, it cannot conflict with Tirumanthiram 6 ('no hard penance without him'), so the tension and its gains are invented.

72 says a gem rolled in mire is still a gem to those who know (அளறாடிக் கண்ணும் மணிமணி யாகிவிடும்); Naladiyar 347 says a sandal of gold and gems is still for the foot and the rich base are known by their deeds. Each states one half of the same rule, that worth does not follow fortune, so the pair teaches more than either, though 72's first line is uncertain.

14 says that the same day he gave the dying dog the nectar he overcame the elephant that frightened Gunamalai; 973 is the elephant's breaking loose (தொடர்பிணி வெளின்முதன் முருக்கி). Summary and event do correspond, but 'planned as a pair of virtues' is the note's gloss and the link only repeats the patikam's own sentence.

107 has the astrologer say a Vidyadhara king will give his daughter; 530 raises the doubt that Vidyadharas and men do not marry (மணவினை முயங்க லில்லென்று), to be answered. 530 does not mention the prophecy, so that the objection tests it is read from the plot, and 'the story's way of making what was foretold pass through argument' is not shown.

605 urges strive at hard penance while still in the body (உடம்பு நீங்காது அருந்தவ முயன்மின்); 724 says body must be nurtured because without it true knowledge cannot be had (மெய்ஞ்ஞானஞ் சேரவு மாட்டார்). Both use the living body as the place for work, but 'spends the body' is read into 605, and the gains offer Tirumular a 'contrast' that is a choice of reading, not stated.

599 has Maruci say the king cannot sleep for fear protection fail; 53 says in the days he guarded the world only Kama's arrows were abroad. 53 says nothing about queens or idle days, so the contrast depends on 611-619, not in the packet, and a courtier's praise beside a narrator's description is no incompatible claim; the same-king identification is unshown.
